clips.syllabus: SQL: joins (inner/outer/self), GROUP BY/HAVING, subqueries
clips.title: Inner join semantics and row multiplication on non-unique keys
clips.hook: What an inner join keeps, drops, and why non-unique join columns duplicate rows.
clips.summary: An inner join emits a combined row for every pair of rows whose ON columns match, and drops unmatched rows from both sides. If the join columns are not unique, every matching pair produces an output row, so rows are duplicated.
clips.videoTitle: 6 SQL Joins you MUST know! (Animated + Practice)

quiz.question: Table A has 3 rows with key=5 and table B has 2 rows with key=5. How many rows with key=5 does A INNER JOIN B ON A.key=B.key produce?
quiz.explanation: An inner join emits one output row per matching pair, so non-unique keys give 3 × 2 = 6 rows.

clips.syllabus: MAC layer, Ethernet vs Wi-Fi (CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA), switches vs routers vs hubs
clips.title: Ethernet Frame: Preamble, SFD and MAC Addressing
clips.hook: How the 7-byte preamble and SFD synchronize the receiver before the destination MAC begins.
clips.summary: The preamble is 7 bytes of alternating 1/0 for clock synchronization. The SFD (10101011) marks the frame start, with its final two 1s signalling that the destination MAC follows. The frame then carries 6-byte destination and source MAC addresses, with ARP used to find the destination MAC.

quiz.question: What is the role of the last two bits (11) of the Ethernet SFD byte 10101011?
options: They set the payload length
They indicate the frame is multicast
They signal that the destination MAC address field follows
They give the CRC of the preamble
quiz.explanation: The SFD breaks the alternating pattern with 11, marking the end of synchronization and the start of the destination address.

clips.syllabus: MAC layer, Ethernet vs Wi-Fi (CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA), switches vs routers vs hubs
clips.title: Ethernet Type/Length, Padding, CRC and the PHY Header
clips.hook: Which Ethernet fields belong to layer 2 and which, preamble and SFD, belong to the physical layer.
clips.summary: The 2-byte length/type field indicates the data length or upper-layer protocol. Padding fills short payloads, and a 4-byte CRC trailer detects errors. The preamble and SFD are treated as the physical-layer header used for synchronization.

clips.syllabus: MAC layer, Ethernet vs Wi-Fi (CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA), switches vs routers vs hubs
clips.title: Ethernet Minimum and Maximum Frame Sizes
clips.hook: Derive the 64-byte minimum and 1518-byte maximum Ethernet frame from payload bounds and overhead.
clips.summary: Payload ranges from 46 to 1500 bytes. Adding 18 bytes of overhead (6+6+2+4 for the addresses, type/length and CRC) gives a minimum frame of 64 bytes (512 bits) and a maximum of 1518 bytes (12144 bits). The preamble and SFD are excluded from the count.

quiz.question: Excluding the preamble and SFD, what is the maximum Ethernet frame size when the payload is 1500 bytes?
options: 1526 bytes
1518 bytes
1514 bytes
1500 bytes
quiz.explanation: 1500 payload + 6 dest + 6 src + 2 type/length + 4 CRC = 1518 bytes.

clips.syllabus: MAC layer, Ethernet vs Wi-Fi (CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA), switches vs routers vs hubs
clips.title: Ethernet Addresses: Unicast, Multicast, Broadcast
clips.hook: How the least significant bit of the first byte of a MAC address separates unicast from multicast, and what FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF means.
clips.summary: A MAC address is 48 bits (6 bytes, 12 hex digits). The LSB of the first byte is 0 for unicast and 1 for multicast. An all-ones address (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) is broadcast and a switch forwards it to all nodes.

quiz.question: How does an Ethernet destination address indicate multicast?
options: LSB of the first byte is 1
All 48 bits are 1
MSB of the first byte is 1
LSB of the last byte is 1
quiz.explanation: The least significant bit of the first byte is 0 for unicast and 1 for multicast. Broadcast is the special all-ones case.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Branch delay slots: executing a fixed instruction after a branch
clips.hook: How a delay slot hides control-hazard latency regardless of branch outcome, and why a branch can't sit in it.
clips.summary: With n delay slots, n instructions after the branch always execute before control transfers, whether taken (to target) or not taken (to PC+4). The slot is filled with a control-flow-independent instruction to cover the branch resolution latency, and it must not itself be a branch.

quiz.question: In a pipeline with one branch delay slot, what happens to the instruction placed in the slot?
options: It is squashed whenever the branch is resolved
It executes only if the branch is taken
It executes only if the branch is not taken
It executes regardless of the branch outcome, before control transfers
quiz.explanation: The delay slot instruction is fetched without knowledge of the outcome and always executes; the compiler must choose one that is safe on both paths.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Compiler scheduling of delay slots: three fill options
clips.hook: Compare filling the delay slot from before the branch, from the target, or from the fall-through path.
clips.summary: The compiler fills slots by (a) moving an independent instruction from before the branch, always useful, (b) copying from the branch target, good if usually taken, or (c) taking from the fall-through path, good if usually not taken. Options b and c are probabilistic, so option a is the best choice.

quiz.question: Why is filling the delay slot with an instruction from before the branch generally preferred over target or fall-through instructions?
options: It eliminates data hazards in the pipeline
It always makes the branch predicted correctly
It is independent of the branch so it is useful on both outcomes
It removes the need for a compiler
quiz.explanation: An instruction from before the branch executes on either path, while target and fall-through instructions are useful only if the branch goes that way.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Stalls, CPI and pipeline speedup limits
clips.hook: Why branch frequency and a 2-cycle penalty keep pipeline speedup below the number of stages.
clips.concept: CPI and pipeline speedup with stalls
clips.summary: Ideal CPI of 1 gives speedup equal to pipeline depth. Stall cycles from data and control hazards raise CPI above 1, so speedup falls below depth. With about 20% branches and a 2-cycle penalty when resolved in execute, the effect is significant.

quiz.question: Why does pipeline speedup fall below the pipeline depth in a real 5-stage pipeline?
options: Stall cycles from hazards raise CPI above 1
Fewer instructions are fetched per cycle
Instruction count increases
Clock period grows with stages
quiz.explanation: Speedup is roughly depth/(1+stall cycles per instruction), so stalls from hazards reduce it below depth.

clips.syllabus: Casts: static_cast vs dynamic_cast vs reinterpret_cast, RTTI
clips.title: C++ casts add compile-time checks, not new power
clips.hook: Why static_cast, reinterpret_cast, const_cast exist if C-style casts can do it all.
clips.summary: The four C++ casts (static, reinterpret, dynamic, const) add no conversion ability beyond a C-style cast, except dynamic_cast's runtime check. They make intent explicit, are greppable, and let the compiler reject impossible conversions, such as int to an unrelated class type. Only reinterpret_cast permits int* to unrelated-class* type punning, whereas a C-style cast silently does whatever works.

quiz.question: Why is static_cast<Foo*>(&someInt) rejected by the compiler while (Foo*)&someInt compiles?
options: C-style casts call a hidden constructor of Foo
static_cast checks at compile time that the conversion is plausible; a C-style cast falls back to reinterpret_cast semantics
static_cast performs a runtime type check that fails
int pointers can never be converted to class pointers in any form
quiz.explanation: static_cast only allows well-defined type conversions. A C-style cast tries static_cast, then falls back to reinterpret_cast and const_cast combinations, so it compiles.

clips.syllabus: Casts: static_cast vs dynamic_cast vs reinterpret_cast, RTTI
clips.title: dynamic_cast: runtime-checked downcast returning null
clips.hook: How dynamic_cast verifies a Base* really points to the target type, unlike static_cast.
clips.summary: A Base* that actually points to a Derived is cast to an unrelated sibling class. static_cast or a C-style cast would just blindly produce a bad pointer, but dynamic_cast checks the real object type at runtime and yields nullptr on failure. You can test the result to branch on the true dynamic type, at the cost of runtime overhead.

quiz.question: Base* b points to a Derived object. What does dynamic_cast<Other*>(b) return, where Other is an unrelated class derived from Base?
options: An exception is always thrown
A dangling pointer reinterpreting the Derived memory
nullptr, because the runtime type check fails
A compile error
quiz.explanation: For pointer casts, dynamic_cast uses runtime type info to verify the target type and returns nullptr on failure. Only reference casts throw std::bad_cast.

clips.syllabus: MAC layer, Ethernet vs Wi-Fi (CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA), switches vs routers vs hubs
clips.title: How a Layer 2 Switch Learns its MAC Address Table
clips.hook: Switches build their forwarding table by recording the source MAC and ingress port of every frame.
clips.summary: A switch starts with an empty MAC address table. For every frame that arrives, it records the frame's source MAC against the ingress port, so it learns where each host is reachable without any configuration.
clips.videoTitle: How L2 Switches Use MAC Addresses

quiz.question: A freshly powered-on switch receives a frame on port 1 with source MAC A and destination MAC B. What does it learn from this frame?
options: A is reachable via port 1
B is reachable via port 1
A and B are both on port 1
Nothing, because the table is only populated by ARP
quiz.explanation: Learning uses the source MAC address of each incoming frame and associates it with the port the frame arrived on.

clips.syllabus: MAC layer, Ethernet vs Wi-Fi (CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA), switches vs routers vs hubs
clips.title: Switch Forwarding: Unicast, Broadcast and Unknown-Unicast Flooding
clips.hook: How a switch uses its MAC table to forward selectively, and when it must flood a frame.
clips.summary: If the destination MAC is in the table, the switch forwards the frame only out the matching port. This is why it is more efficient than a hub. A broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) or an unknown unicast is flooded out every port except the one it arrived on.
clips.videoTitle: How L2 Switches Use MAC Addresses

quiz.question: When does a Layer 2 switch flood a frame out all ports except the ingress port?
options: When the destination is the broadcast address or an unknown unicast address
Only when the source MAC is not yet in the table
Whenever the frame is larger than the MTU
Only when the destination MAC is a known unicast address
quiz.explanation: Broadcast frames must reach every host. For an unknown unicast the switch does not know the egress port, so it floods the frame until the destination replies and is learned.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Precise State: Draining Older Instructions, Flushing Younger
clips.hook: What the pipeline must do on an exception so the architectural state looks sequential.
clips.summary: On an exception at instruction i3, older instructions (i1, i2) must complete, while i3 and all younger instructions are flushed and never fetched. Then EPC is saved, further interrupts are disabled, and control jumps to the handler address (from the cause register or a vector), giving a precise machine state.

quiz.question: Instruction i3 raises an exception in a pipelined processor. Which action gives a precise state?
options: Flush i1, i2 and i3 and restart from i1
Let i1 and i2 complete, flush i3 and younger instructions, save EPC, and jump to the handler
Let all in-flight instructions, including those younger than i3, complete before calling the handler
Call the handler at once and let in-flight older instructions finish in the background
quiz.explanation: Precise state means all instructions before the faulting one have committed and none after it have modified state.

clips.syllabus: Pipelining: 5 stages, hazards (structural, data, control), forwarding, stalls
clips.title: Exceptions at Different Pipeline Stages and Their Priority
clips.hook: Each of the 5 stages can fault, so how does the pipeline order simultaneous exceptions?
clips.summary: Each stage has its own exception type: invalid PC in fetch, illegal opcode in decode, overflow in execute, bad data address in memory. On an exception, that stage and all younger instructions are killed. If one instruction has several exceptions, the earliest stage wins. Asynchronous interrupts are different: the current instruction is allowed to reach write-back first.

quiz.question: An instruction has both an invalid PC and an illegal opcode. Which exception is handled, and why?
options: The illegal opcode, because it is detected later and is more specific
Neither, because the pipeline stalls instead
The invalid PC, because earlier-stage exceptions take priority and make later ones meaningless
Both are handled simultaneously by the handler
quiz.explanation: If the PC is invalid, the fetched instruction is meaningless, so the earlier-stage exception overrides later ones.

clips.syllabus: Gradients, convexity, gradient descent, learning rate; SGD vs momentum vs Adam
clips.title: Why plain GD oscillates in elongated valleys
clips.hook: Oscillation across a ravine caps the learning rate and slows progress along the useful direction.
clips.summary: On elongated contours, gradient descent bounces across the steep direction while crawling along the shallow one. Oscillation limits the usable learning rate, since a larger one diverges, so you want slower learning vertically and faster horizontally.

quiz.question: Why does oscillation across the steep axis of an elongated quadratic limit gradient descent?
options: It increases the loss at the minimum
It only occurs with mini-batches
It makes the gradient zero in the shallow direction
It forces a small learning rate, since a larger one would diverge, which slows progress along the shallow axis
quiz.explanation: The steep direction bounds the stable step size, so the shallow direction progresses slowly.

clips.syllabus: Gradients, convexity, gradient descent, learning rate; SGD vs momentum vs Adam
clips.title: Momentum: exponentially weighted average of gradients
clips.hook: How the velocity update cancels oscillating components and keeps consistent ones.
clips.summary: Momentum keeps v = beta*v + (1-beta)*grad and updates w with alpha*v. Oscillating components of opposite sign average toward zero, while consistent components along the valley remain large, giving a straighter and faster path.

quiz.question: Why does momentum damp vertical oscillations but not horizontal progress?
options: It lowers the learning rate in the horizontal direction
Vertical gradients alternate in sign and average near zero, while horizontal gradients consistently point the same way
It zeroes gradients below a threshold
It computes second derivatives
quiz.explanation: The exponential average cancels alternating components and preserves consistent ones.

clips.syllabus: Gradients, convexity, gradient descent, learning rate; SGD vs momentum vs Adam
clips.title: Momentum in practice: beta, bias correction, scaling
clips.hook: Choosing beta=0.9, skipping bias correction, and how dropping (1-beta) rescales the learning rate.
clips.summary: Beta=0.9 averages roughly the last 10 gradients and is robust. Bias correction is usually skipped as the average warms up quickly. Omitting the (1-beta) factor scales v by 1/(1-beta), so alpha must be retuned, and tuning beta then also changes the effective step scale.

quiz.question: If momentum is written v = beta*v + g (without 1-beta), how does it compare to the (1-beta) form?
options: It removes the need for a learning rate
They are identical in all cases
v is larger by 1/(1-beta), so the learning rate must be scaled accordingly
v is smaller by a factor of beta
quiz.explanation: The steady-state magnitude is g/(1-beta) versus g, so alpha must be rescaled.

clips.syllabus: SQL: joins (inner/outer/self), GROUP BY/HAVING, subqueries
clips.title: Subqueries in FROM: derived tables to reuse expressions
clips.hook: Use a FROM-clause subquery as a derived table to compute an expression once and reuse it.
clips.summary: A subquery in FROM yields a relation that the outer query treats like a table, so a computed column such as a scaled GPA can be referenced several times. Most SQL implementations require an alias for the derived table.

quiz.question: Why place the scaled-GPA computation in a FROM-clause subquery rather than repeating it in WHERE?
options: It forces the optimizer to materialize the result on disk
It makes the expression evaluate faster by definition
It removes the need for any alias
The subquery produces a derived relation whose computed column can be referenced by name in the outer query
quiz.explanation: The FROM subquery defines a derived table whose columns, including computed ones, can be referenced by name. Aliasing is normally required, and no performance guarantee follows.

clips.syllabus: SQL: joins (inner/outer/self), GROUP BY/HAVING, subqueries
clips.title: Scalar subqueries in SELECT must return one value
clips.hook: A SELECT-clause subquery fills one cell, so it must return exactly one row, or it errors.
clips.summary: A correlated subquery in SELECT is evaluated per outer row, for example the max GPA of applicants to each college. It must return exactly one value, because it fills a single cell. Returning multiple rows, such as applicant names, raises a 'subquery returns more than one row' error.

quiz.question: Why does a SELECT-clause subquery listing all applicant names per college raise an error?
options: DISTINCT is missing
Subqueries are not allowed to reference outer tables
The college table lacks a key
Scalar subqueries must produce exactly one value to fill one result cell
quiz.explanation: A subquery in SELECT is used as a scalar expression. Multiple rows leave the value for the cell ambiguous, so the DBMS raises an error.

clips.syllabus: Branch prediction
clips.title: 1-bit Branch History Table: indexing and aliasing
clips.hook: How a tagless PC-indexed 1-bit table predicts branches, and why aliasing is harmless to correctness.
clips.summary: A BHT is a tagless table of 1-bit entries indexed by low PC bits (ignoring the 2 byte-offset bits), storing the last outcome. Aliasing between branches only hurts performance, not correctness, since predictions are verified at execution; it helps only if target is known before direction.

quiz.question: Why can a branch history table omit tags without compromising program correctness?
options: The prediction is only a hint and is verified when the branch executes, so aliasing only costs performance
The compiler guarantees that no two branches share an index
The table is flushed on every branch
Aliased entries are always identical across branches
quiz.explanation: Predictions are checked at execution; a wrong prediction from aliasing triggers recovery, affecting only performance.

clips.syllabus: Branch prediction
clips.title: Why 1-bit predictors fail on nested loops; 2-bit bimodal FSM
clips.hook: Two mispredictions per inner-loop run with 1 bit, and how a 2-bit state machine fixes it.
clips.summary: For an inner loop executing 16 times, a 1-bit predictor mispredicts at exit and again on the next entry, giving 14/16 = 88% accuracy versus the branch's 94% bias. A 2-bit predictor changes its prediction only after two consecutive mispredictions, so the loop-exit costs only one miss.

quiz.question: An inner loop branch is taken 15 times then not taken once, repeatedly. How many mispredictions per outer iteration in steady state for 1-bit vs 2-bit predictors?
options: 1 and 0
2 and 1
1 and 1
2 and 2
quiz.explanation: 1-bit: miss at exit and miss at next first iteration. 2-bit: stays in a taken state after the exit miss, so only one miss.

clips.syllabus: Branch prediction
clips.title: 2-bit saturating counters and n-bit generalization
clips.hook: The counter view of the bimodal predictor and why more than 2 bits doesn't help much.
clips.summary: The 2-bit scheme can be implemented as a saturating counter incremented on taken and decremented on not-taken, bounded in 0 to 3. Predict taken when the counter is at or above half its max; n-bit counters give little gain over 2 bits, so most processors use 2 bits.

quiz.question: In a 2-bit saturating counter predictor, what is the prediction when the counter value is 2?
options: Depends on the previous branch
Undefined
Not taken
Taken
quiz.explanation: Counter values 2 and 3 (at or above half the max) predict taken.

clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Von Neumann Model: Stored Program and Sequential Processing
clips.hook: Unified memory, bit interpretation by access stage, and PC-driven sequential execution.
clips.summary: The two defining properties are the stored-program concept (unified linear memory where bits are interpreted as instruction or data based on the stage accessing them) and sequential instruction processing governed by the PC. The PC advances by instruction size except for control-transfer instructions, which implement loops and conditionals.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: In a von Neumann machine, how does the hardware decide whether a memory word is an instruction or data?
options: By the opcode field of the word itself always
By the stage of processing accessing it (fetch vs. data access)
A tag bit stored with every word
By the memory region's separate physical bank
quiz.explanation: Memory is unified and untyped; interpretation depends on whether it is accessed in instruction fetch or operand fetch.

clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Dataflow vs Von Neumann: No PC, Token-Driven Firing
clips.hook: What if instructions fire when operands are ready, with no program counter?
clips.summary: In the dataflow model there is no program counter; an instruction is fetched and executed when all its input operands (tokens) are available, and each instruction names its consumers. This exposes much more parallelism than the von Neumann model's sequential ordering.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: What determines when an instruction executes in a pure dataflow machine?
options: A compiler-inserted schedule slot
The program counter reaching it
Clock cycle count modulo pipeline depth
Availability of all its input operand tokens
quiz.explanation: Firing is triggered by operand availability; there is no PC.

clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Why Multi-Cycle Beats Single-Cycle: Slowest Stage vs Slowest Instruction
clips.hook: Split instruction processing into stages so the cycle time follows the slowest stage.
clips.summary: The six phases of the instruction cycle all fit in one cycle in a single-cycle machine, whereas multi-cycle machines can spend several cycles per phase. The cycle time is set by the slowest stage rather than the slowest instruction, though both still follow sequential von Neumann semantics.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

clips.syllabus: Von Neumann architecture, fetch-decode-execute cycle
clips.title: Iron Law of Performance: Single vs Multi-Cycle
clips.hook: Time = instructions × CPI × cycle time, applied to microarchitecture choices.
clips.summary: Execution time is instruction count times average CPI times cycle time. Single-cycle has CPI=1 but a long cycle; multi-cycle gets short cycles and a low average CPI by weighting frequent cheap instructions, giving two independent optimization knobs.
clips.videoTitle: Digital Design & Computer Architecture - Lecture 11: Microarchitecture I (ETH Zürich, Spring 2020)

quiz.question: A single-cycle machine has which iron-law property?
options: CPI above 1
CPI of 1 with a long cycle time
CPI varies, short cycle
Fewer instructions
quiz.explanation: Every instruction takes one cycle, but the cycle must fit the longest instruction.

clips.syllabus: Bayes' rule, base rates; common distributions
clips.title: Accurate test, low PPV: sensitivity, specificity, base rate
clips.hook: Why a test with 90% sensitivity and 91% specificity gives only ~1/11 chance of disease given positive.
clips.concept: Positive predictive value and base rate
clips.summary: With 1% prevalence, 9 true positives and 89 false positives give PPV = 9/98 ≈ 1/11. Test accuracy is two numbers (sensitivity, specificity) and neither alone gives P(disease | positive); the base rate dominates.
clips.videoTitle: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule

quiz.question: In a population with 1% prevalence, a test has 90% sensitivity and ~9% false positive rate. Why is P(disease | positive) only about 1/11?
options: Specificity and sensitivity cancel each other
Sensitivity is too low to detect disease
False positives from the large healthy group (~89) greatly outnumber true positives (~9)
The test is biased toward healthy patients
quiz.explanation: Because the healthy group is 99x larger, even a 9% false positive rate yields about 89 false positives versus 9 true positives, so PPV = 9/98.

clips.syllabus: Bayes' rule, base rates; common distributions
clips.title: Bayes factor: tests update priors, not give answers
clips.hook: Reduce sensitivity and FPR to a single likelihood ratio and use it to approximate posteriors.
clips.summary: A test updates a prior; the relevant number for a positive result is the Bayes factor = sensitivity / false positive rate (here 10). For small priors, multiplying by it approximates the posterior, but it fails for large priors (10% gives 53%, not 100%).
clips.videoTitle: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule

quiz.question: Why does the rule 'posterior ≈ prior × Bayes factor' fail for a 10% prior with Bayes factor 10?
options: The false positive rate becomes zero
Bayes factor changes with the prior
Sensitivity must be recomputed
It treats probabilities as if they were unbounded; it only holds approximately when the prior is small
quiz.explanation: Multiplication is exact for odds, not probabilities. For small probabilities odds ≈ probability, but at 10% it overshoots (true answer 9/17 ≈ 53%).

clips.syllabus: Bayes' rule, base rates; common distributions
clips.title: Bayes' rule in odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × BF
clips.hook: Why Bayesian updating is exactly multiplication once you switch from probabilities to odds.
clips.summary: Odds are positives to negatives; filtering to positive results scales the diseased count by sensitivity and the healthy count by FPR, so posterior odds = prior odds × Bayes factor exactly. Examples: 1:99 → 10:99 (~1/11), 1:9 → 10:9 (53%), BF 90 gives ~48%.
clips.videoTitle: The medical test paradox, and redesigning Bayes' rule

quiz.question: Prior probability is 10% (odds 1:9) and the Bayes factor is 10. What is the posterior probability?
quiz.explanation: Posterior odds = 1:9 × 10 = 10:9, so probability = 10/19 ≈ 53%.
